title: Tabea Iseli: Animal Crossing meets Roguelite Dungeon Crawler: The genre mixture of Grimoire Groves
speaker: Tabea Iseli
talk_title: Animal Crossing meets Roguelite Dungeon Crawler: The genre mixture of Grimoire Groves
description: During the peak of the Covid pandemic, a small indie game studio from Switzerland set out to take their favorite genre - roguelite dungeon crawlers - and transfer it into a cozy, colorful and comforting world. After all, the real world out there is already scary enough, so at least our favorite video games should be a place we want to escape to, right? Over the past four years, this vision manifested itself in Grimoire Groves, a roguelite game about witches, friendship, mythical creatures and growing plants. The talk tackles the surprising similarities between farming/life sims and roguelite dungeon crawlers by explaining how Grimoire Groves mixes cute Animal Crossing-like villagers and friendship systems with dungeon crawler action mechanics.

segments.text: Our next speaker is Tabea Iseli is the founder and game director of Stardust, a Swiss indie game
studio creating diverse games for a diverse audience. I will let you kick it off. I want
to let you get into "Animal Crossing meets Roguelite Dungeon Crawler: The surprising
genre mixture behind Grimoire Groves." TABEA: Since we are at Roguelike Celebration
and I am giving a talk, it probably comes to nobody's surprise that roguelikes are one of
my favorite genres and it was always a dream for me to create one myself. Back in 2020 when
we were talking about the concept for our second game that dream started to become a reality. We
wanted to create a non-violent dungeon with growing plants with magic. To explain how we
came to this decision, let's travel back to the year 2020. A year probably most of us spent alone
at home in some fashion. For gaming 2020 was a huge year. We had Animal Crossing, new horizons,
huge hits, which also for many people were some kind of a shining light through the pandemic. If
I remember correctly, it was also the year when whole some direct took the gaming world by storm
and made it career wholesome and cozy games were here to stay. Roguelike games, on the other hand,
were still a staple of indie game as they arguably are still today because they have this captivating
formula that never grows old. The anticipation of what you might encounter on the next draw,
the hope of finding the right components for your build to click, sometimes also the thrill
of living on the edge, and at least for roguelites the solace that even if you fail you at least made
a step towards your goal. We ask ourselves the question if it would be possible to re-create
this captivateing roguelike elements but not in a traditional it is a dark dungeon and you
have to slay monster kind of setting but rather colorful, cute, and cozy world. We came up with
the concept where you as a witch would grow plant creatures with magic and materials you find on
your journey and help the local foresters. It is still a traditional Dungeon Crawler so you
are exploring a procedurally generated map, cast spells on plant creatures that replace the enemies
in a traditional roguelike game. You also can buy boons that, hopefully, will synergize well and
help you get through the whole run where you will encounter a bus fight. Our vision was wizard of
legends meets adventure time. But we also leaned into some aspect of farming games because on one
hand they are popular with our target audience but share similarities with roguelike and Dungeon
Crawler mechanics. If you think about it, both are about collecting resources, both have have these
freedom for players to choose their own approaches and priorities, and in both genres players are
working over several runs or game days to reach their next goal. As a plus, the farming aspects
were also helping us to explain the non-violent aspects of our game because players could
understand the concept of watering plants with magic. This mixture with farming games especially
helped us with meta-progression. As an example our spell tree in the game is a literal tree.
That's just not a silly pun that went too far but rather we made the whole upgrading and unlocking
system a garden in your home base. Unlocks are plants that you can put into your garden. After
you start with an empty overgrown plot of land it will slowly turn into a pretty home over time
which at the same time also is a representation of your capabilities in the game. This is one
aspect that our players loved from the beginning and of course they wanted to see more stuff like
that. One feature that we sadly were not able to implement was their wish that they could place
these objects freely in the garden. Even though it is super hard, we wanted to have some areas
where woe we wanted to go the extra mile for the players. While our wizard of legend meets
adventure time some found appeal with players but they pushed toward the Hades or cult of the lamb
meets Animal Crossing direction. No pressure. It is not like these were some of the biggest games
in the last few years. Suddenly a whole bunch of players were throwing errands that and despite the
impossibility of meeting these high expectations as just a small indie team we still decided we
wanted to try to bring some of these wishes to the game for our players. Admittedly a lot of things
I wanted to see in the game were very unexpected for us. For example, one thing that players wanted
to see more of was story and we actually hot it would be the other way around. We had all these
uncommon non-violent action mechanics that we had to explain which generated a lot of dialogue and
we thought that this might be a complete turn off for players because after all neither roguelikes
or farming sims are super rich in story. Many roguelikes barely have a story at all. It is like,
yeah, go slay these evil monsters. Farming sims don't have an intricate overarching story but the
meat is in the players and background. Our players were totally going for it. They loved the story.
They loved the elemental spirits. The quarrel among sibblings, dialogue, corky characters,
and most of all the humor. Despite roguelike genre usually being the opposite of story rich, we
wanted to accommodate our player's wishes because it was one way to flesh out the game but it
was also a way to help players understand the roguelike genre because it isn't super simple
to understand how roguelikes work if you have never played one before. Of course,
when we were talking about player wishes and players enjoying our characters and drawing
inspiration from Animal Crossing, befriending characters was a huge topic. Since friendship,
luckily was already at the core of our story, we were more than happy to implement that theme into
our game mechanics but we wanted to stay true with the roguelike core. We took shock MPCs and you can
befriend them doing fun little mini games giving additional choices in the shop and a discount.
We also created cute homes for the characters and they can new love in permanently in your forest if
you befriend them. We took the bus plants and put them into the backyard of set characters and give
players additional benefits in the bus fight if they already befriended the character. Yes, that
means we have do fights in the game ebon -- even those are cozy because you are helping friends
harvesting the fruits of the huge plants in the backyard. That's kind of the story of how we
started with a concept for a non-violent roguelike game and it more turned into Animal Crossing esc
Dungeon Crawler. To me the story is more than just the story of our game. It also highlights
what I like so much about this genre. How amazing and versatile it is. I am 100% sure we will see
more innovative iterations and reinventions of the roguelike genre. After all, even since we
started with Grimoire Groves we realized we are not at all alone in the non-violent or
cozy roguelike space. To show some examples, we have moon drop which showed us it is possible to
create a non-violent farming roguelike. I also saw worlds greatest pub which is a game I discovered
at this conference. I am so hyped because it is a roguelike game about dog shows of all things.
That's just amazing. I would also like to talk about Dave the diver because that showed us the
cozy crowd is ready to embrace roguelike games if they are made for a cozy crowd. Long story short,
I am sure that there is a lot to look forward to in the future of roguelike games. I am also
very happy Grimoire Groves will probably not be the last ever cute and cozy roguelike game.
ALEXEI: Very exciting. Thank you. Super cute. If people have questions, we probably have time for
one at least. But yeah, kicking things off. I think what's really interesting there is
how it sounds like as a team you dug why people are asking for what they are and asking for and
in other genres what purpose is this serving? What is the interaction with the villagers and the part
that matter? The sense of building a community like Animal Crossing where it
feels good you build up friends close by and figuring out how to copy that. It is
interesting when you go genre to genre you don't want to just copy and paste. Similar to roguelikes
where you need a progression mechanic and that could be a garden or an UI. I think that's
interesting how you've considered the elements of those different genres and how to blend them.
TABEA: Yup. I also think when we started the gaming world looked differently in 2020. It
was really important for us to give our target audience a voice because back then they were
not really heard as an audience. There are not a lot of games out there for them. So we made the
conscious decision that we kind of want to do this participation design where we would go throughout
as early as possible to players and ask them, you know, what kind of things would you like to see in
the game? How should it look? They decided on the art stuff for example. They also came up with the
name for our game. We tried to keep them in the loop and ask them as much as possible within the
boundaries of what is possible for us to do as an indie studio with a set budget basically.
ALEXEI: That's great. I think that really relevant -- the early access type development. It is more
and more common. It has that back and forth. And reminds me, I don't know what year it was,
we had a talk from one of the devs of shattered pixel dungeon for mobile who I believe talked
about the process of taking user feedback. When people were like I want to see Gamlen
in the game from lord of the rings. It is like well, can't do that. That's IP. So
that kind of mediating back and forth. It is good that you found a way to do that. Sounds
like you have a really positive community. TABEA: Oh, absolutely, yes. They are amazing.
ALEXEI: Excellent. Thank you. It is great shout-out world's goodest pub.
TABEA: Looking forward so much to that game. ALEXEI: People can check out Grimoire Groves
in the Steam sale. I am sure we have a link to it. Thank you very much, Tabea.
